title: 45-Day Identification Strategy
name: 45-Day Identification Strategy
metaTitle: 45-Day Identification Strategy in San Jose, CA
metaDescription: 45-day 1031 identification strategy for San Jose owners, screening replacement candidates before closing given how tight this metro's inventory runs.

sections.html: Forty-five calendar days is what a San Jose exchanger gets to put replacement candidates in writing, and in a metro where land scarcity keeps the reliable pool of tradeable buildings thin, that window closes faster than the calendar suggests. After running exchanges through cycles of Golden Triangle expansion and downtown redevelopment pressure, we start building the identification list before the relinquished property is even under contract, since waiting for a signed sale agreement to begin the search almost always costs owners their strongest candidates.

sections.heading: Why the Clock Starts Before Most Owners Expect
sections.html:
The 45-day window begins on the closing date of the relinquished property, not the date you decide to exchange or the date you first talk to a qualified intermediary. In San Jose, where single-tenant buildings along the Golden Triangle and industrial parcels north of Berryessa rarely sit on the market long, owners who wait until after closing to start looking are often working from a thin, already-picked-over list by day 20.

We treat the identification search as a pre-closing task, not a post-closing one, so the letter that goes to the QI on day 40 reflects real diligence instead of a rushed guess.

sections.heading: Building a Short List Before You List the Relinquished Property
sections.html:
Because San Jose's tradeable inventory of single-tenant NNN buildings, transit-village multifamily, and North San Jose flex product turns over slowly, we start screening candidates as soon as an owner signals intent to sell, sometimes months before the relinquished property goes under contract. That gives time to run rent rolls, check zoning against any planned Coyote Valley or greenfield parcels under consideration, and rule out buildings that look available but are quietly under a letter of intent already.

This early screening also means we can rank candidates by how realistic their closing timeline actually is, rather than by list price alone, so the final 45-day letter reflects buildings that can plausibly close by day 180, rather than ones that merely photograph well in a listing.

sections.heading: What the Identification Letter Has to Include
sections.html:
The letter to the qualified intermediary has to meet a specific bar well beyond a list of addresses you happen to like. It needs:

  • Legal description or unambiguous street address for each candidate
  • Signature and delivery to the QI directly, rather than to the broker or seller alone
  • Delivery on or before midnight of day 45, with no weekend or holiday extension
  • Compliance with either the three-property or 200% identification rule
  • Written confirmation of receipt from the qualified intermediary

A letter that satisfies every item on this list except the delivery deadline still fails the exchange, which is why we treat day 40 as the real target rather than day 45.

sections.heading: How Downtown Redevelopment Pressure Thins the Pool
sections.html:
Large-scale projects near Diridon Station have pulled capital and attention toward downtown in a way that ripples through pricing on comparable single-tenant and flex buildings across the rest of the city. When a major redevelopment announcement moves a submarket, sellers who might have listed a North First Street or Golden Triangle building often pull back to wait and see, shrinking the live inventory an exchanger has to choose from during exactly the weeks the 45-day clock is running.

We track these announcements as part of the identification search, because a building that looked available in week one can disappear from the market in week three for reasons that have nothing to do with the deal itself.

sections.heading: The Cost of Missing Day 45
sections.html: If the identification letter isn't delivered, signed, and in the QI's hands by midnight on day 45, the exchange fails regardless of how close you were to a deal. There is no grace period for a building's inspection running long or a broker's email arriving a day late. We build in a buffer, aiming for delivery by day 40, so a last-minute title issue or a QI question about wording doesn't turn into a missed deadline.

faqs.q: When exactly does the 45-day clock start?
faqs.a: It starts on the closing date of the relinquished property, the same day the 180-day exchange period begins. Both windows run concurrently, not one after the other.

faqs.q: Can I extend the 45 days if I haven't found a replacement yet?
faqs.a: No, there is no extension available for ordinary market conditions, including a thin San Jose inventory. Relief has historically been limited to federally declared disasters, and even then only under specific IRS guidance.

faqs.q: What if I identify a property and later find something better?
faqs.a: You can only acquire from the properties formally identified in writing by day 45. If something better surfaces after that, it can't become a replacement property in this exchange unless it was already on the list.

faqs.q: Does a verbal description of a property count as identification?
faqs.a: No. The IRS requires an unambiguous written description, typically a legal description or street address, delivered to the qualified intermediary before the deadline. A verbal mention to your broker or QI does not satisfy the requirement.

faqs.q: How many properties should I put on the list given how tight this market is?
faqs.a: There's no universal number, but given how quickly single-tenant and flex inventory moves here, most owners are better served identifying more than the bare minimum and using the 200% rule if the combined value requires it. Confirm the right count with your qualified intermediary based on your actual exchange value.
